lesson.title: Implicit Functions: When y Is Tangled Up With x Instead of Isolated
lesson.summary: An implicit function defines a relationship between x and y through an equation that is never solved for y alone, yet y can still behave like a function of x, at least locally, wherever the equation traces out a well defined curve.
lesson.body:
Every function studied so far in this course has been explicit: y = f(x), with y by itself on one side and a formula in x on the other, so plugging in a number for x immediately produces the corresponding y. Many natural relationships, however, are not handed to us in that tidy form. The equation x^2 + y^2 = 25 relates x and y without ever isolating y, yet for many values of x it still determines y, at least up to a choice between two possible values, positive and negative, once x is restricted to the interval from negative 5 to 5.

A relationship like this is called an implicit function: y is implicitly determined by the equation, even though the equation is not solved for y explicitly. Sometimes an implicit relationship can actually be solved for y using algebra, turning it into one or more explicit functions; for x^2+y^2=25, solving for y gives y = sqrt(25-x^2) or y = -sqrt(25-x^2), two separate explicit functions covering the upper and lower halves of the circle. Other times, algebra cannot isolate y at all, such as in y^5 + xy = 3, where no combination of standard algebraic moves gets y alone on one side, and the implicit form is the only practical way to describe the relationship.

Consider the explicit function obtained by solving x^2+y^2=25 for the upper half, y = sqrt(25-x^2) = (25-x^2)^(1/2). Using the general power rule with u = 25-x^2 and u' = -2x, dy/dx = (1/2)(25-x^2)^(-1/2) times (-2x) = -x(25-x^2)^(-1/2) = -x / sqrt(25-x^2). At x = 3, y = sqrt(25-9) = sqrt(16) = 4, and dy/dx = -3/sqrt(16) = -3/4. This matches the geometric expectation for a circle: the tangent line to a circle is always perpendicular to the radius at that point, and the radius from the origin to (3,4) has slope 4/3, so a perpendicular tangent line should have slope -3/4, exactly what the derivative gives, a satisfying agreement between algebra and geometry.

Notice that computing this derivative required solving for y first, which worked here because the circle equation happens to be solvable using a square root. This strategy quietly breaks down for equations like y^5+xy=3, where no algebraic manipulation isolates y as a formula in x; differentiating such equations directly, without ever solving for y, is exactly the technique that implicit differentiation is built to handle, treating y as an unnamed function of x throughout and applying the chain rule to every y term as it appears.

Recognizing when a relationship is implicit, and understanding that y can still be a legitimate function of x even without an explicit formula, at least on some restricted piece of the curve, is the conceptual foundation the next topic builds on. The circle example shows both sides of the coin: implicit functions can sometimes be converted to explicit ones for practice and verification, but the real power of implicit reasoning shows up precisely when that conversion is not available at all.
